title: More blessed to give (Acts 20:17–38)
hook: Paul's farewell at Miletus; they weep and kneel on the shore

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eutychus, asleep in the window while Paul talked till dawn. Your line was even Paul went on. Whose long story did you sit through kindly? Day five hundred fifty-four.

A beach at Miletus, on the coast of Asia. Paul is in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, so he doesn't go up to Ephesus, where he spent about three years. Instead he sends for the elders of the Ephesian church to come down to the shore. They make the journey down to meet him. And he gives them a farewell. He tells them plainly: I don't know what will happen to me in Jerusalem, except that prison and hardship are waiting. And you will not see my face again.
screen: `A BEACH AT MILETUS.` → `THE ELDERS OF EPHESUS.` → `YOU WILL NOT SEE MY FACE AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Paul's farewell sounds like a man setting his affairs in order. He reminds them how he lived among them: serving the Lord with humility and tears, holding nothing back, teaching in public and from house to house. He tells them to keep watch over the flock, like shepherds. Then he holds up his hands. I've coveted no one's silver or gold or clothing. These hands, he says, worked for my own needs and for those who were with me. And then he gives them a saying of Jesus. In the Douay-Rheims: "remember the word of the Lord Jesus, how he said: It is a more blessed thing to give, rather than to receive." Here's the surprise. Those words of Jesus aren't in any of the four Gospels. Matthew, Mark, Luke and John never record them. This is a saying of Jesus preserved only here, in Paul's mouth, passed along by Luke. One sentence of Jesus, kept by people who remembered it. Notice what Paul does with it. He isn't asking the elders for money. He's showing them his own work-worn hands and saying: this is how to lead. Give. Then the ending. Paul kneels down on the shore and prays with them all. They weep, embrace him, and kiss him, grieving most of all, the text says, because he told them they would not see his face again. And they walk him to the ship.
screen: `HUMILITY, TEARS, NOTHING HELD BACK.` · `THESE HANDS WORKED FOR MY NEEDS.` · `A SAYING FOUND IN NO GOSPEL.` · `KNEELING ON THE SHORE.` · then, large: `MORE BLESSED TO GIVE, RATHER THAN TO RECEIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give something today. Settle, and breathe. Look at your hands, the way Paul held up his. What have they given lately? Now think of one thing you could give today, freely, without being asked. Not necessarily money. Time, a meal, a compliment you meant to say, help with a task, something you own that someone else needs more. Picture handing it over and walking away without waiting for thanks. Notice how that feels. If you pray, you can offer your hands for whatever giving the day brings. The bell holds the time.
Blessed. The word Jesus used in a saying kept only by Paul, on a beach at Miletus: it is more blessed to give than to receive. Today's word.
Your line: coveted no one's silver. Today, do your work honestly, with open hands, not wanting what isn't yours. Day five hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics practice almsgiving, one of the three traditional disciplines of Lent alongside prayer and fasting, and give to the poor through parish collections and works of mercy throughout the year.

myth: it is more blessed to give than to receive is in one of the Gospels
it isn't in any of the four Gospels. Paul quotes it as Jesus' words in Acts.
Paul asked the elders for money in his farewell
he showed his own hands and said they had worked for his needs.
the elders wept because they would not see him again
that grieved them most of all, the text says.

fork.setup: you're Paul, saying goodbye forever to people you've taught for three years. what do you leave them?
options: a list of rules to follow.
your example, and a saying of Jesus about giving.
fork.reveal: he points to how he lived, holds up his working hands, and quotes Jesus: it is a more blessed thing to give, rather than to receive.

original.note: Greek: blessed, the same word family as the Beatitudes. more blessed is it to give.

trapdoor: what you thought: a proverb from the Gospels.
what it means: a saying of Jesus remembered by Paul at a tearful farewell, as he holds up his own work-worn hands.
what a scholar hears: sayings of Jesus found outside the four Gospels are called agrapha, unwritten sayings. Acts 20:35 is a standard New Testament example.

sources.quoted: remember the word of the Lord Jesus, how he said: It is a more blessed thing to give, rather than to receive.

notes: 'About three years' in Ephesus follows Acts 20:31; Miletus to Ephesus roughly thirty miles (about fifty km) as traveled; confirm.
'The only speech in Acts that Paul makes to Christians': a common observation; confirm.
Agrapha: confirm term and that Acts 20:35 is the standard example.

Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS: Acts 20:35 was quoted from the KJV; now the Douay-Rheims ('It is a more blessed thing to give, rather than to receive'), verified; screen and fork follow. Cut 'some thirty miles' (not in the text), 'the only speech in Acts that Paul makes to Christians', 'one of the most tender scenes in Acts', 'almost lost' and 'the best known' agraphon.
